note.note:
Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old woman (hotel housekeeper) with 3–4 months of progressively painful, cracked, and intermittently itchy palmar skin, worse recently and impairing work; history and occupational exposures strongly suggest hand dermatitis (likely irritant contact) without systemic symptoms; PMH notable for type 2 diabetes; plan includes trigger avoidance (consistent glove use), topical steroid cream, and frequent emollients with follow-up in 10–14 days.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Painful, cracked, itchy skin on the palms of both hands; worse over the last several days.
- Onset/duration: Began ~3–4 months ago; progressively worsened; unable to work for the past 3 days due to pain.
- Character: Marked dryness with fissuring/cracks; intermittent pruritus; occasional bleeding only after scratching (no spontaneous bleeding).
- Location: Primarily palms; patient notes mild generalized dryness (legs) but not severe.
- Exacerbating/initiating factors: Occupational exposure to cleaning products; inconsistent glove use; started new hotel housekeeping job ~4 months ago.
- Relieving measures tried: OTC emollient (E45) without benefit; oral antihistamine without benefit.
- Associated symptoms/ROS:
  - Denies fever or temperature.
  - Denies nausea/vomiting.
  - Denies bowel or urinary issues.
  - Otherwise feels well; appetite intact.
- Additional context: Patient reports she “doesn’t hydrate very much.”

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
  - Medications: Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - No prior diagnosed skin conditions (no known eczema/dermatitis).

Social History:
- Occupation: Hotel housekeeper (bedrooms, bathrooms, corridors); frequent exposure to cleaning chemicals; inconsistent glove use; job change ~4 months ago.
- Work impact: Unable to work for last 3 days due to hand pain.
- Tobacco: Nonsmoker.
- Alcohol: A couple of pints per week.
- No other substance use mentioned.

Family History:
- Diabetes in family.
- No known family history of skin disease, asthma, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Physical Examination:
- (No vitals or physical exam findings documented.)

Investigations:
- None mentioned.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Hand dermatitis, likely irritant contact dermatitis related to occupational exposures (cleaning agents, wet work), with baseline xerosis; allergic contact component possible.
  - Evidence: Onset after new housekeeping job; frequent exposure to cleaning products; inconsistent glove use; palmar-dominant dryness, fissuring, pain, pruritus; no systemic symptoms; lack of response to antihistamine and basic emollient.
  - Plan:
    - Trigger avoidance: Wear protective gloves consistently when cleaning and minimize direct contact with cleaning chemicals.
    - Topical therapy:
      - Topical steroid cream prescribed (specific agent/dose/route/frequency not documented).
      - Stronger emollients: Apply liberally 3–4 times daily for the next couple of weeks.
    - Follow-up: Reassess in 10–14 days; return sooner if worsening or spreading, or if not improving.
    - Prescription logistics: Prescription to be sent to patient’s pharmacy.
- Issue 2: Type 2 diabetes mellitus.
  - Current visit impact: Not the primary focus today; acknowledged as comorbidity that may contribute to dry skin. No changes to management documented in this visit.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Irritant contact hand dermatitis (High likelihood):
  - Strong temporal link to new hotel housekeeping job with repeated exposure to cleaning chemicals and inconsistent glove use; classic symptoms of painful, cracked, itchy palms; antihistamine ineffective.
- Allergic contact dermatitis to occupational agents (Moderate likelihood):
  - Exposure to potential allergens in cleaning agents or gloves; pruritus and chronicity fit; may coexist with irritant dermatitis, though no specific allergen identified.
- Asteatotic/xerotic eczema (Moderate likelihood):
  - Baseline generalized dryness and diabetes may impair skin barrier and healing; distribution primarily palmar and strong occupational link favor irritant dermatitis as primary driver.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements:
  - No vitals or physical examination description (e.g., erythema, scaling pattern, vesicles, weeping, signs of infection, unilateral vs bilateral).
  - No documentation of specific topical steroid name or dosing instructions.
  - No details on specific cleaning products or glove types/materials.
  - No assessment of glycemic control or diabetic skin complications.
  - Allergies documented only as “no known”; no latex/glove material sensitivities specifically addressed.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality: Some incomplete/overlapping speech but overall history understandable; no exam provided.
